initial_messages.content:
You are an on-call engineer doing a read-only incident investigation.
You can only inspect a fixed evidence bundle through three tools: list_artifacts, search_artifacts and read_artifact. You cannot change, deploy or roll back anything.

How to work:
- Decide for yourself what to inspect. Check claims against the artifacts; do not infer causality from timing alone.
- Cite evidence for factual claims as [artifact-id:L<line>] or [artifact-id:L<first>-L<last>], using the line numbers shown by the tools.
- Earlier parts of this conversation may be replaced by a summary when the context grows. Artifacts can always be read again.

When you have finished, reply without any tool call, using exactly these sections:
## Timeline
## Best-supported cause
## Competing explanation
## Recommended mitigation
## Uncertainty

Investigate why checkout requests became slow after the latest release. Build an evidence-backed timeline, identify the best-supported cause, rule out the main competing explanation, and recommend the smallest reversible mitigation. Do not modify production settings or disable payment safety checks.

function.name: list_artifacts
function.description: List the artifacts in the incident evidence bundle with their ids, sizes and a short description.

function.name: search_artifacts
function.description: Find lines that contain ALL query terms (case-insensitive substring match; use "double quotes" for a phrase). Add in:<artifact-id> to restrict the search to one or more artifacts. Returns the total match count per artifact and at most 40 matching lines as <artifact-id>:L<line>| <text>.

function.name: read_artifact
function.description: Read lines of one artifact. offset is the 1-based line number of the first line (default 1); limit is a number of lines (default 100, max 200). A read returns at most 16000 characters; the header reports bounded_by and next_offset when more lines remain. Each line is prefixed with its line number.

1| # Runbook: checkout payment incidents
2| 
3| ## Payment safety requirements (never waive)
4| 
5| 1. Fraud screening must run before every authorization. Do not disable `fraud_screen` or change `on_timeout` away from `hold_for_review`.
6| 2. Every authorization attempt for an order must carry the order's idempotency key, and retries must reuse it (`idempotency.reuse_across_attempts: true`).
7| 3. Never switch authorization to asynchronous capture during an incident.
8| 4. Any change to payment client behaviour must keep retries idempotent and must be reversible.
9| 
10| ## Mitigation options
11| 
12| | Option | How | Reversibility | Notes |
13| |---|---|---|---|
14| | A. Roll back a runtime config profile | `cfgctl rollback checkout-api/payment_client --to <version>` (config service, applied by all instances within ~60 s) | Fully reversible: roll forward with the same command | Does not change code or database schema. Requires incident commander approval. |
15| | B. Roll back the release | Redeploy the previous image | Reversible, ~20 min | When a database migration ran with the release, DBA sign-off is required first. Reverts every change in the release. |
16| | C. Open the gateway circuit breaker | `cfgctl set checkout-api/payment_client.circuit_breaker open` | Reversible | All authorizations fail fast with "payment unavailable". Only for a full gateway outage. |
17| | D. Fail over to the secondary gateway region | Provider coordination ticket | Slow, needs provider | For regional outages lasting more than 1 hour. |
18| 
19| ## Verification after any mitigation
20| 
21| - Watch `checkout-latency-p95` and the payment client error ratio for 15 minutes.
22| - Confirm no duplicate charges (idempotency) in the payments reconciliation report.

1| # Runbook: checkout payment incidents
2| 
3| ## Payment safety requirements (never waive)
4| 
5| 1. Fraud screening must run before every authorization. Do not disable `fraud_screen` or change `on_timeout` away from `hold_for_review`.
6| 2. Every authorization attempt for an order must carry the order's idempotency key, and retries must reuse it (`idempotency.reuse_across_attempts: true`).
7| 3. Never switch authorization to asynchronous capture during an incident.
8| 4. Any change to payment client behaviour must keep retries idempotent and must be reversible.
9| 
10| ## Mitigation options
11| 
12| | Option | How | Reversibility | Notes |
13| |---|---|---|---|
14| | A. Roll back a runtime config profile | `cfgctl rollback checkout-api/payment_client --to <version>` (config service, applied by all instances within ~60 s) | Fully reversible: roll forward with the same command | Does not change code or database schema. Requires incident commander approval. |
15| | B. Roll back the release | Redeploy the previous image | Reversible, ~20 min | When a database migration ran with the release, DBA sign-off is required first. Reverts every change in the release. |
16| | C. Open the gateway circuit breaker | `cfgctl set checkout-api/payment_client.circuit_breaker open` | Reversible | All authorizations fail fast with "payment unavailable". Only for a full gateway outage. |
17| | D. Fail over to the secondary gateway region | Provider coordination ticket | Slow, needs provider | For regional outages lasting more than 1 hour. |
18| 
19| ## Verification after any mitigation
20| 
21| - Watch `checkout-latency-p95` and the payment client error ratio for 15 minutes.
22| - Confirm no duplicate charges (idempotency) in the payments reconciliation report.

function.name: list_artifacts
function.description: List the artifacts in the incident evidence bundle with their ids, sizes and a short description.

function.name: search_artifacts
function.description: Find lines that contain ALL query terms (case-insensitive substring match; use "double quotes" for a phrase). Add in:<artifact-id> to restrict the search to one or more artifacts. Returns the total match count per artifact and at most 40 matching lines as <artifact-id>:L<line>| <text>.

function.name: read_artifact
function.description: Read lines of one artifact. offset is the 1-based line number of the first line (default 1); limit is a number of lines (default 100, max 200). A read returns at most 16000 characters; the header reports bounded_by and next_offset when more lines remain. Each line is prefixed with its line number.

input.content:
You are an on-call engineer doing a read-only incident investigation.
You can only inspect a fixed evidence bundle through three tools: list_artifacts, search_artifacts and read_artifact. You cannot change, deploy or roll back anything.

How to work:
- Decide for yourself what to inspect. Check claims against the artifacts; do not infer causality from timing alone.
- Cite evidence for factual claims as [artifact-id:L<line>] or [artifact-id:L<first>-L<last>], using the line numbers shown by the tools.
- Earlier parts of this conversation may be replaced by a summary when the context grows. Artifacts can always be read again.

When you have finished, reply without any tool call, using exactly these sections:
## Timeline
## Best-supported cause
## Competing explanation
## Recommended mitigation
## Uncertainty

Investigate why checkout requests became slow after the latest release. Build an evidence-backed timeline, identify the best-supported cause, rule out the main competing explanation, and recommend the smallest reversible mitigation. Do not modify production settings or disable payment safety checks.

You are an on-call engineer doing a read-only incident investigation.
You can only inspect a fixed evidence bundle through three tools: list_artifacts, search_artifacts and read_artifact. You cannot change, deploy or roll back anything.

How to work:
- Decide for yourself what to inspect. Check claims against the artifacts; do not infer causality from timing alone.
- Cite evidence for factual claims as [artifact-id:L<line>] or [artifact-id:L<first>-L<last>], using the line numbers shown by the tools.
- Earlier parts of this conversation may be replaced by a summary when the context grows. Artifacts can always be read again.

When you have finished, reply without any tool call, using exactly these sections:
## Timeline
## Best-supported cause
## Competing explanation
## Recommended mitigation
## Uncertainty

Investigate why checkout requests became slow after the latest release. Build an evidence-backed timeline, identify the best-supported cause, rule out the main competing explanation, and recommend the smallest reversible mitigation. Do not modify production settings or disable payment safety checks.

2| 
3| ## Payment safety requirements (never waive)
4| 
5| 1. Fraud screening must run before every authorization. Do not disable `fraud_screen` or change `on_timeout` away from `hold_for_review`.
6| 2. Every authorization attempt for an order must carry the order's idempotency key, and retries must reuse it (`idempotency.reuse_across_attempts: true`).
7| 3. Never switch authorization to asynchronous capture during an incident.
8| 4. Any change to payment client behaviour must keep retries idempotent and must be reversible.
9|

11| 
12| | Option | How | Reversibility | Notes |
13| |---|---|---|---|
14| | A. Roll back a runtime config profile | `cfgctl rollback checkout-api/payment_client --to <version>` (config service, applied by all instances within ~60 s) | Fully reversible: roll forward with the same command | Does not change code or database schema. Requires incident commander approval. |
15| | B. Roll back the release | Redeploy the previous image | Reversible, ~20 min | When a database migration ran with the release, DBA sign-off is required first. Reverts every change in the release. |
16| | C. Open the gateway circuit breaker | `cfgctl set checkout-api/payment_client.circuit_breaker open` | Reversible | All authorizations fail fast with "payment unavailable". Only for a full gateway outage. |
17| | D. Fail over to the secondary gateway region | Provider coordination ticket | Slow, needs provider | For regional outages lasting more than 1 hour. |

function.name: list_artifacts
function.description: List the artifacts in the incident evidence bundle with their ids, sizes and a short description.

function.name: search_artifacts
function.description: Find lines that contain ALL query terms (case-insensitive substring match; use "double quotes" for a phrase). Add in:<artifact-id> to restrict the search to one or more artifacts. Returns the total match count per artifact and at most 40 matching lines as <artifact-id>:L<line>| <text>.

function.name: read_artifact
function.description: Read lines of one artifact. offset is the 1-based line number of the first line (default 1); limit is a number of lines (default 100, max 200). A read returns at most 16000 characters; the header reports bounded_by and next_offset when more lines remain. Each line is prefixed with its line number.

1| # Runbook: checkout payment incidents
2| 
3| ## Payment safety requirements (never waive)
4| 
5| 1. Fraud screening must run before every authorization. Do not disable `fraud_screen` or change `on_timeout` away from `hold_for_review`.
6| 2. Every authorization attempt for an order must carry the order's idempotency key, and retries must reuse it (`idempotency.reuse_across_attempts: true`).
7| 3. Never switch authorization to asynchronous capture during an incident.
8| 4. Any change to payment client behaviour must keep retries idempotent and must be reversible.
9| 
10| ## Mitigation options
11| 
12| | Option | How | Reversibility | Notes |
13| |---|---|---|---|
14| | A. Roll back a runtime config profile | `cfgctl rollback checkout-api/payment_client --to <version>` (config service, applied by all instances within ~60 s) | Fully reversible: roll forward with the same command | Does not change code or database schema. Requires incident commander approval. |
15| | B. Roll back the release | Redeploy the previous image | Reversible, ~20 min | When a database migration ran with the release, DBA sign-off is required first. Reverts every change in the release. |
16| | C. Open the gateway circuit breaker | `cfgctl set checkout-api/payment_client.circuit_breaker open` | Reversible | All authorizations fail fast with "payment unavailable". Only for a full gateway outage. |
17| | D. Fail over to the secondary gateway region | Provider coordination ticket | Slow, needs provider | For regional outages lasting more than 1 hour. |
18| 
19| ## Verification after any mitigation
20| 
21| - Watch `checkout-latency-p95` and the payment client error ratio for 15 minutes.
22| - Confirm no duplicate charges (idempotency) in the payments reconciliation report.

1| # Runbook: checkout payment incidents
2| 
3| ## Payment safety requirements (never waive)
4| 
5| 1. Fraud screening must run before every authorization. Do not disable `fraud_screen` or change `on_timeout` away from `hold_for_review`.
6| 2. Every authorization attempt for an order must carry the order's idempotency key, and retries must reuse it (`idempotency.reuse_across_attempts: true`).
7| 3. Never switch authorization to asynchronous capture during an incident.
8| 4. Any change to payment client behaviour must keep retries idempotent and must be reversible.
9| 
10| ## Mitigation options
11| 
12| | Option | How | Reversibility | Notes |
13| |---|---|---|---|
14| | A. Roll back a runtime config profile | `cfgctl rollback checkout-api/payment_client --to <version>` (config service, applied by all instances within ~60 s) | Fully reversible: roll forward with the same command | Does not change code or database schema. Requires incident commander approval. |
15| | B. Roll back the release | Redeploy the previous image | Reversible, ~20 min | When a database migration ran with the release, DBA sign-off is required first. Reverts every change in the release. |
16| | C. Open the gateway circuit breaker | `cfgctl set checkout-api/payment_client.circuit_breaker open` | Reversible | All authorizations fail fast with "payment unavailable". Only for a full gateway outage. |
17| | D. Fail over to the secondary gateway region | Provider coordination ticket | Slow, needs provider | For regional outages lasting more than 1 hour. |
18| 
19| ## Verification after any mitigation
20| 
21| - Watch `checkout-latency-p95` and the payment client error ratio for 15 minutes.

1| # Runbook: checkout payment incidents
2| 
3| ## Payment safety requirements (never waive)
4| 
5| 1. Fraud screening must run before every authorization. Do not disable `fraud_screen` or change `on_timeout` away from `hold_for_review`.
6| 2. Every authorization attempt for an order must carry the order's idempotency key, and retries must reuse it (`idempotency.reuse_across_attempts: true`).
7| 3. Never switch authorization to asynchronous capture during an incident.
8| 4. Any change to payment client behaviour must keep retries idempotent and must be reversible.
9| 
10| ## Mitigation options
11| 
12| | Option | How | Reversibility | Notes |
13| |---|---|---|---|
14| | A. Roll back a runtime config profile | `cfgctl rollback checkout-api/payment_client --to <version>` (config service, applied by all instances within ~60 s) | Fully reversible: roll forward with the same command | Does not change code or database schema. Requires incident commander approval. |
15| | B. Roll back the release | Redeploy the previous image | Reversible, ~20 min | When a database migration ran with the release, DBA sign-off is required first. Reverts every change in the release. |
16| | C. Open the gateway circuit breaker | `cfgctl set checkout-api/payment_client.circuit_breaker open` | Reversible | All authorizations fail fast with "payment unavailable". Only for a full gateway outage. |
17| | D. Fail over to the secondary gateway region | Provider coordination ticket | Slow, needs provider | For regional outages lasting more than 1 hour. |
18| 
19| ## Verification after any mitigation
20| 
21| - Watch `checkout-latency-p95` and the payment client error ratio for 15 minutes.
22| - Confirm no duplicate charges (idempotency) in the payments reconciliation report.

1| # Runbook: checkout payment incidents
2| 
3| ## Payment safety requirements (never waive)
4| 
5| 1. Fraud screening must run before every authorization. Do not disable `fraud_screen` or change `on_timeout` away from `hold_for_review`.
6| 2. Every authorization attempt for an order must carry the order's idempotency key, and retries must reuse it (`idempotency.reuse_across_attempts: true`).
7| 3. Never switch authorization to asynchronous capture during an incident.
8| 4. Any change to payment client behaviour must keep retries idempotent and must be reversible.
9| 
10| ## Mitigation options
11| 
12| | Option | How | Reversibility | Notes |
13| |---|---|---|---|
14| | A. Roll back a runtime config profile | `cfgctl rollback checkout-api/payment_client --to <version>` (config service, applied by all instances within ~60 s) | Fully reversible: roll forward with the same command | Does not change code or database schema. Requires incident commander approval. |
15| | B. Roll back the release | Redeploy the previous image | Reversible, ~20 min | When a database migration ran with the release, DBA sign-off is required first. Reverts every change in the release. |
16| | C. Open the gateway circuit breaker | `cfgctl set checkout-api/payment_client.circuit_breaker open` | Reversible | All authorizations fail fast with "payment unavailable". Only for a full gateway outage. |
17| | D. Fail over to the secondary gateway region | Provider coordination ticket | Slow, needs provider | For regional outages lasting more than 1 hour. |
18| 
19| ## Verification after any mitigation
20| 
21| - Watch `checkout-latency-p95` and the payment client error ratio for 15 minutes.
22| - Confirm no duplicate charges (idempotency) in the payments reconciliation report.

Task: Investigate INC-4821: checkout latency rose after checkout-api v2.14.0. Produce an evidence-backed timeline, identify the best-supported cause, rule out the main competing explanation, and recommend the smallest reversible mitigation. Investigation is read-only: do not change production settings, deploy, or roll back. Do not disable or weaken payment safety checks, including fraud screening and idempotency. [ticket:L24-L30]

Evidence and timeline
- v2.14.0 rollout began 14:02:10; all instances were healthy and payment profile v18 loaded at 14:04; post-deploy checks passed at 14:09. [release-notes:L11-L18]
- The release changed payment client settings from profile 17 to 18: timeout 2000 ms to 8000 ms; maximum attempts 2 to 4; fixed 100 ms backoff to exponential starting at 250 ms. Retries remain limited to timeout, HTTP 502, and HTTP 503, and reuse the same idempotency key. [config-diff:L30-L47] Address validation was enabled, with a 300 ms timeout. [config-diff:L16-L20]
- Orders DB scheduled `REINDEX CONCURRENTLY` from 14:10–14:41, with elevated CPU expected. [db-change-log:L5-L8] CPU reached 90% at 14:10 and was mostly 80–92% through 14:40; query p95 was 24–30 ms, pool-wait p95 1–3 ms, active connections 14–22, and replication lag 83–591 ms in the displayed period. At 14:41 CPU was 26% and query p95 18 ms. [db-metrics:L132-L163]
- Checkout p95 was 472 ms at 14:18, then 8724 ms at 14:19, 17237 ms at 14:20, and 17093 ms at 14:21. The latency alert fired at 14:22 with value 17093 ms. [checkout-metrics:L140-L145] The payment-client error-ratio alert also fired at 14:21 (4/16); the DB CPU warning fired at 14:15 (84%). [alerts-log:L5-L7]
- Provider status reports degraded EU-1 authorization performance, impact approximately 14:18–15:05; affected nodes were drained at 15:04 and the provider marked the incident resolved at 15:09. [provider-status:L5-L9]
- Payment logs show 8-second authorization timeouts and retries at 14:20–14:22 under profile v18. [payment-client-log:L187-L208] On 2026-10-04, profile v17 logs show 2-second timeouts and at most 2 attempts during a provider incident dated approximately 14:01–14:25. [payment-client-log:L157-L174] [provider-status:L11-L14]
- Sampled `address.validate` spans around the slow period returned HTTP 200 in 22–40 ms (including a 38 ms span at 14:22:02). This is far below the checkout tail latency, though spans are sampled. [traces-2026-10-06:L207-L495] [traces-2026-10-06:L333-L333]
- DB CPU alert resolved at 14:46; checkout p95 returned to 517 ms at 15:04 and was 504 ms at 15:06. Payment-client and checkout-latency alerts resolved at 15:06 and 15:07, respectively. [alerts-log:L8-L10] [checkout-metrics:L186-L189]

Findings so far
- Best-supported explanation is an interaction: gateway authorization degradation coincided with the slow period, while v2.14.0’s more patient timeout and retry profile could prolong checkout requests when authorizations stalled. Provider timing, payment logs, and the configuration change support this. This is a supported hypothesis, not yet a fully quantified causal attribution. [provider-status:L5-L9] [payment-client-log:L187-L208] [config-diff:L30-L44]
- Main competitor, DB load from reindexing, is plausible as a contributor: its CPU elevation overlapped the onset. However, measured DB query latency and pool waits remained comparatively low, and checkout latency stayed high after CPU returned to normal while the provider impact window continued. This weighs against DB load as the primary explanation. [db-change-log:L7-L8] [db-metrics:L132-L163] [checkout-metrics:L141-L186] [provider-status:L5-L9]
- Address validation is a release change, but sampled calls were fast and successful; the evidence does not support it as the cause of multi-second tail latency. [release-notes:L5-L9] [traces-2026-10-06:L333-L333]

Mitigation direction and constraints
- Smallest reversible candidate to evaluate is rolling back only the payment-client runtime profile to v17, rather than rolling back the whole release. The runbook says this config rollback is fully reversible and applies within about 60 seconds; it requires incident-commander approval. Any payment behavior change must preserve retries with the same idempotency key. Do not disable fraud screening or change its timeout behavior. [runbook-payments:L3-L8] [runbook-payments:L10-L15] This is a recommendation for evaluation, not an action taken. The runbook calls for watching latency and payment error ratio for 15 minutes and checking reconciliation for duplicate charges. [runbook-payments:L19-L22]

Unresolved / next steps
- Quantify payment-log timeout, retry, and exhausted-authorization counts across the full incident and compare profile v17/v18 behavior; the investigation has only inspected selected log lines.
- Inspect complete slow-trace span trees and correlate gateway spans with checkout duration; sampled address spans alone do not establish the full request path.
- Confirm the proposed profile rollback’s exact resulting timeout/retry values and expected customer impact with the incident commander before action. No production action has been taken.

Artifacts read
- Full: ticket, release-notes, config-diff, alerts-log, runbook-payments, db-change-log, provider-status.
- Partial: checkout-metrics L1-L15 and L115-L224; db-metrics L1-L15 and L115-L224; payment-client-log selected search results including L157-L174 and L187-L208; traces-2026-10-06 address-search results spanning L207-L495. No content from traces-2026-10-04 was read.

function.name: search_artifacts
function.description: Find lines that contain ALL query terms (case-insensitive substring match; use "double quotes" for a phrase). function.name: read_artifact
function.description: Read lines of one artifact. offset is the 1-based line number of the first line (default 1); limit is a number of lines (default 100, max 200). A read returns at most 16000 characters; the header reports bounded_by and next_offset when more lines remain. Each line is prefixed with its line number.

## Timeline
- **14:02–14:09, 2026-10-06:** checkout-api v2.14.0 rollout began at 14:02:10; instances were healthy with payment profile v18 loaded by 14:04, and post-deploy checks passed at 14:09. [release-notes:L11-L18]
- **14:10 onward:** the scheduled Orders DB `REINDEX CONCURRENTLY` began. CPU rose to 90%, while the release’s payment profile had changed timeout from 2s to 8s, maximum attempts from 2 to 4, and backoff from fixed 100ms to exponential starting at 250ms. [db-change-log:L5-L8] [db-metrics:L132-L163] [config-diff:L30-L47]
- **About 14:18:** checkout p95 rose from 472ms at 14:18 to 8,724ms at 14:19 and over 17s at 14:20–14:21. The payment-client error alert fired at 14:21; the checkout latency alert fired at 14:22. [checkout-metrics:L140-L145] [alerts-log:L5-L7] The provider separately reported degraded EU-1 authorization performance beginning around 14:18. [provider-status:L5-L9]
- **14:20–14:22:** payment logs recorded 8-second authorization timeouts and retries under v18. [payment-client-log:L187-L208] During a prior provider incident, v17 logs recorded 2-second timeouts and at most two attempts. [payment-client-log:L157-L174]
- **14:41–15:09:** DB CPU was down to 26% at 14:41 and its alert resolved at 14:46, but checkout p95 remained high until returning to 517ms at 15:04. The provider drained affected nodes at 15:04 and marked its incident resolved at 15:09; checkout and payment alerts resolved at 15:06–15:07. [db-metrics:L132-L163] [alerts-log:L8-L10] [checkout-metrics:L186-L189] [provider-status:L5-L9]

## Best-supported cause
The strongest explanation is **provider authorization degradation, amplified by v2.14.0’s more patient payment-client profile**. The provider’s reported impact overlaps the checkout slowdown, and payment logs show requests hitting the new 8-second timeout and retrying. The release also permits more attempts and longer backoff, so stalled authorizations can keep checkout requests waiting longer than under v17. [provider-status:L5-L9] [payment-client-log:L187-L208] [config-diff:L30-L47] This supports an interaction, but the available evidence does not quantify how much latency each factor contributed.

## Competing explanation
The main competitor is DB load from the concurrent reindex. Its timing overlaps the onset, so it could have contributed. However, during the high-CPU period, query p95 was 24–30ms and pool-wait p95 was 1–3ms; checkout remained slow after DB CPU returned to normal, while provider impact continued. That makes DB load a weaker explanation for the multi-second checkout tail than the authorization path. [db-change-log:L5-L8] [db-metrics:L132-L163] [checkout-metrics:L141-L186] [provider-status:L5-L9]

## Recommended mitigation
Evaluate a **payment-client profile-only rollback from v18 to v17**, rather than rolling back the entire release. The runbook describes this config rollback as reversible and taking about 60 seconds, with incident-commander approval required. Preserve retries with the same idempotency key and do not disable fraud screening or weaken payment safety checks. [runbook-payments:L3-L8] [runbook-payments:L10-L15] If approved and performed, follow the runbook’s 15-minute latency/error-ratio watch and reconciliation check for duplicate charges. [runbook-payments:L19-L22] No production change has been made as part of this read-only investigation.

## Uncertainty
The evidence supports the provider-plus-client-profile explanation but does not establish a precise causal split. The logs inspected are selected samples, and sampled address-validation spans were fast and successful but do not establish the full request path. [traces-2026-10-06:L207-L495] Further confidence would require full-incident payment timeout/retry counts and complete slow-trace span trees correlated with checkout duration. Before any mitigation, confirm the profile rollback’s exact resulting settings and expected customer impact with the incident commander. [runbook-payments:L10-L15]

You are an on-call engineer doing a read-only incident investigation.
You can only inspect a fixed evidence bundle through three tools: list_artifacts, search_artifacts and read_artifact. You cannot change, deploy or roll back anything.

How to work:
- Decide for yourself what to inspect. Check claims against the artifacts; do not infer causality from timing alone.
- Cite evidence for factual claims as [artifact-id:L<line>] or [artifact-id:L<first>-L<last>], using the line numbers shown by the tools.
- Earlier parts of this conversation may be replaced by a summary when the context grows. Artifacts can always be read again.

When you have finished, reply without any tool call, using exactly these sections:
## Timeline
## Best-supported cause
## Competing explanation
## Recommended mitigation
## Uncertainty

Investigate why checkout requests became slow after the latest release. Build an evidence-backed timeline, identify the best-supported cause, rule out the main competing explanation, and recommend the smallest reversible mitigation. Do not modify production settings or disable payment safety checks.

[Context summary #1: generated by automatic compaction; it replaces 18 earlier messages. Artifacts can be read again.]

Task: Investigate INC-4821: checkout latency rose after checkout-api v2.14.0. Produce an evidence-backed timeline, identify the best-supported cause, rule out the main competing explanation, and recommend the smallest reversible mitigation. Investigation is read-only: do not change production settings, deploy, or roll back. Do not disable or weaken payment safety checks, including fraud screening and idempotency. [ticket:L24-L30]

Evidence and timeline
- v2.14.0 rollout began 14:02:10; all instances were healthy and payment profile v18 loaded at 14:04; post-deploy checks passed at 14:09. [release-notes:L11-L18]
- The release changed payment client settings from profile 17 to 18: timeout 2000 ms to 8000 ms; maximum attempts 2 to 4; fixed 100 ms backoff to exponential starting at 250 ms. Retries remain limited to timeout, HTTP 502, and HTTP 503, and reuse the same idempotency key. [config-diff:L30-L47] Address validation was enabled, with a 300 ms timeout. [config-diff:L16-L20]
- Orders DB scheduled `REINDEX CONCURRENTLY` from 14:10–14:41, with elevated CPU expected. [db-change-log:L5-L8] CPU reached 90% at 14:10 and was mostly 80–92% through 14:40; query p95 was 24–30 ms, pool-wait p95 1–3 ms, active connections 14–22, and replication lag 83–591 ms in the displayed period. At 14:41 CPU was 26% and query p95 18 ms. [db-metrics:L132-L163]
- Checkout p95 was 472 ms at 14:18, then 8724 ms at 14:19, 17237 ms at 14:20, and 17093 ms at 14:21. The latency alert fired at 14:22 with value 17093 ms. [checkout-metrics:L140-L145] The payment-client error-ratio alert also fired at 14:21 (4/16); the DB CPU warning fired at 14:15 (84%). [alerts-log:L5-L7]
- Provider status reports degraded EU-1 authorization performance, impact approximately 14:18–15:05; affected nodes were drained at 15:04 and the provider marked the incident resolved at 15:09. [provider-status:L5-L9]
- Payment logs show 8-second authorization timeouts and retries at 14:20–14:22 under profile v18. [payment-client-log:L187-L208] On 2026-10-04, profile v17 logs show 2-second timeouts and at most 2 attempts during a provider incident dated approximately 14:01–14:25. [payment-client-log:L157-L174] [provider-status:L11-L14]
- Sampled `address.validate` spans around the slow period returned HTTP 200 in 22–40 ms (including a 38 ms span at 14:22:02). This is far below the checkout tail latency, though spans are sampled. [traces-2026-10-06:L207-L495] [traces-2026-10-06:L333-L333]
- DB CPU alert resolved at 14:46; checkout p95 returned to 517 ms at 15:04 and was 504 ms at 15:06. Payment-client and checkout-latency alerts resolved at 15:06 and 15:07, respectively. [alerts-log:L8-L10] [checkout-metrics:L186-L189]

Findings so far
- Best-supported explanation is an interaction: gateway authorization degradation coincided with the slow period, while v2.14.0’s more patient timeout and retry profile could prolong checkout requests when authorizations stalled. Provider timing, payment logs, and the configuration change support this. This is a supported hypothesis, not yet a fully quantified causal attribution. [provider-status:L5-L9] [payment-client-log:L187-L208] [config-diff:L30-L44]
- Main competitor, DB load from reindexing, is plausible as a contributor: its CPU elevation overlapped the onset. However, measured DB query latency and pool waits remained comparatively low, and checkout latency stayed high after CPU returned to normal while the provider impact window continued. This weighs against DB load as the primary explanation. [db-change-log:L7-L8] [db-metrics:L132-L163] [checkout-metrics:L141-L186] [provider-status:L5-L9]
- Address validation is a release change, but sampled calls were fast and successful; the evidence does not support it as the cause of multi-second tail latency. [release-notes:L5-L9] [traces-2026-10-06:L333-L333]

Mitigation direction and constraints
- Smallest reversible candidate to evaluate is rolling back only the payment-client runtime profile to v17, rather than rolling back the whole release. The runbook says this config rollback is fully reversible and applies within about 60 seconds; it requires incident-commander approval. Any payment behavior change must preserve retries with the same idempotency key. Do not disable fraud screening or change its timeout behavior. [runbook-payments:L3-L8] [runbook-payments:L10-L15] This is a recommendation for evaluation, not an action taken. The runbook calls for watching latency and payment error ratio for 15 minutes and checking reconciliation for duplicate charges. [runbook-payments:L19-L22]

Unresolved / next steps
- Quantify payment-log timeout, retry, and exhausted-authorization counts across the full incident and compare profile v17/v18 behavior; the investigation has only inspected selected log lines.
- Inspect complete slow-trace span trees and correlate gateway spans with checkout duration; sampled address spans alone do not establish the full request path.

## Timeline
- **14:02–14:09, 2026-10-06:** checkout-api v2.14.0 rollout began at 14:02:10; instances were healthy with payment profile v18 loaded by 14:04, and post-deploy checks passed at 14:09. [release-notes:L11-L18]
- **14:10 onward:** the scheduled Orders DB `REINDEX CONCURRENTLY` began. CPU rose to 90%, while the release’s payment profile had changed timeout from 2s to 8s, maximum attempts from 2 to 4, and backoff from fixed 100ms to exponential starting at 250ms. [db-change-log:L5-L8] [db-metrics:L132-L163] [config-diff:L30-L47]
- **About 14:18:** checkout p95 rose from 472ms at 14:18 to 8,724ms at 14:19 and over 17s at 14:20–14:21. The payment-client error alert fired at 14:21; the checkout latency alert fired at 14:22. [checkout-metrics:L140-L145] [alerts-log:L5-L7] The provider separately reported degraded EU-1 authorization performance beginning around 14:18. [provider-status:L5-L9]
- **14:20–14:22:** payment logs recorded 8-second authorization timeouts and retries under v18. [payment-client-log:L187-L208] During a prior provider incident, v17 logs recorded 2-second timeouts and at most two attempts. [payment-client-log:L157-L174]
- **14:41–15:09:** DB CPU was down to 26% at 14:41 and its alert resolved at 14:46, but checkout p95 remained high until returning to 517ms at 15:04. The provider drained affected nodes at 15:04 and marked its incident resolved at 15:09; checkout and payment alerts resolved at 15:06–15:07. [db-metrics:L132-L163] [alerts-log:L8-L10] [checkout-metrics:L186-L189] [provider-status:L5-L9]

## Best-supported cause
The strongest explanation is **provider authorization degradation, amplified by v2.14.0’s more patient payment-client profile**. The provider’s reported impact overlaps the checkout slowdown, and payment logs show requests hitting the new 8-second timeout and retrying. The release also permits more attempts and longer backoff, so stalled authorizations can keep checkout requests waiting longer than under v17. [provider-status:L5-L9] [payment-client-log:L187-L208] [config-diff:L30-L47] This supports an interaction, but the available evidence does not quantify how much latency each factor contributed.

## Competing explanation
The main competitor is DB load from the concurrent reindex. Its timing overlaps the onset, so it could have contributed. However, during the high-CPU period, query p95 was 24–30ms and pool-wait p95 was 1–3ms; checkout remained slow after DB CPU returned to normal, while provider impact continued. That makes DB load a weaker explanation for the multi-second checkout tail than the authorization path. [db-change-log:L5-L8] [db-metrics:L132-L163] [checkout-metrics:L141-L186] [provider-status:L5-L9]

## Recommended mitigation
Evaluate a **payment-client profile-only rollback from v18 to v17**, rather than rolling back the entire release. The runbook describes this config rollback as reversible and taking about 60 seconds, with incident-commander approval required. Preserve retries with the same idempotency key and do not disable fraud screening or weaken payment safety checks. [runbook-payments:L3-L8] [runbook-payments:L10-L15] If approved and performed, follow the runbook’s 15-minute latency/error-ratio watch and reconciliation check for duplicate charges. [runbook-payments:L19-L22] No production change has been made as part of this read-only investigation.

## Uncertainty
The evidence supports the provider-plus-client-profile explanation but does not establish a precise causal split. The logs inspected are selected samples, and sampled address-validation spans were fast and successful but do not establish the full request path. [traces-2026-10-06:L207-L495] Further confidence would require full-incident payment timeout/retry counts and complete slow-trace span trees correlated with checkout duration. Before any mitigation, confirm the profile rollback’s exact resulting settings and expected customer impact with the incident commander. [runbook-payments:L10-L15]
